chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ya'qub ibn Yazid, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from al-Hakam ibn Miskin, from Qutaybah al-A'sha, who said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), 'I recite the Quran, and a gift is sent to me, so I accept it.' He said, 'No.' I said, 'If I do not make it a condition (for the teaching),' he said, 'Do you see if you had not taught him, would he have sent you a gift?' I said, 'No.' He said, 'Then do not accept it.'
Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The meaning in this report is preference (karahah) rather than prohibition (hazr), because abstaining from such is more worthy and superior, even if it is not forbidden.
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on accepting gifts in exchange for teaching the Quran?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies that gifts given specifically as compensation for Quranic instruction are to be avoided to prevent the perception of commercializing religious knowledge, a principle rooted in the hadith's logical deduction that if the teaching were absent, the gift would not be given. While the ruling is classified as disliked (karahah) rather than strictly forbidden (haram), it underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on preserving the spiritual purity of teaching by distinguishing between voluntary charity and transactional payment. This distinction encourages believers to prioritize voluntary acceptance of gifts while remaining mindful of the intent behind them.
